text: Report cost next to every quality or speed result, in real money rather than proxies (parameter count, instance size).
pitfall: Gains bought with unreported spending

text: When two metrics trade off (cost vs accuracy, cost vs latency), show the Pareto frontier instead of a single winner.
pitfall: Ranking that ignores the trade-off

text: Include simple, cheap baselines (e.g. retry or a smaller option) so complex candidates must beat them on cost too.
pitfall: Complexity mistaken for progress

text: Split fixed costs (setup, one-off) from variable costs (per run, per request), state the usage volume assumed, and give a total cost of ownership over a stated period when hardware or licences are involved (TPC uses three years, maintenance included).
pitfall: Conclusions that flip at real volumes or over time

text: Record each price with its date and where it can be obtained (public price page, plan, sales channel).
pitfall: Silent staleness and unverifiable prices

text: Report price/performance (cost per unit of result) together with the raw performance and the raw cost, never alone.
pitfall: A ratio hiding that one side is unusable

text: For metered services, report three things: the pricing model assumed, the resources actually used, and the amount actually charged (billing granularity can make them differ).
pitfall: Costs computed from list prices that the bill does not match

text: Record the raw usage behind every cost (tokens, requests, compute hours, seats) so anyone can recompute it when prices change.
pitfall: Cost comparisons that expire with the next price change

text: Bar charts start at zero; any exception must be disclosed in the chart itself.
pitfall: Exaggerated differences

text: Dot and line charts may use a non-zero baseline when zero is arbitrary or a meaningful change would be invisible, but only with the range set by V8.
pitfall: Both flattening and inflating effects

text: Do not rely on axis-break markers to fix a truncated axis; readers are still misled.
pitfall: False sense of honesty
proved_by: no axis breaks in the generator

text: Always show absolute values, not only ratios or relative numbers; for a speedup, state the base case and its absolute value.
pitfall: Hiding results that are bad or irrelevant in absolute terms

text: Summarize with the right mean: arithmetic for costs (time, energy, money), harmonic for rates (ops/s); never average ratios, summarize the underlying costs or rates instead; only if those are unavailable, use the geometric mean of normalized scores.
pitfall: Meaningless or flattering averages

text: Include a limitations section listing what was not tested.
pitfall: Over-generalized conclusions

text: Give every quantity a unit, and make it unambiguous: count vs rate (flop vs flop/s), binary vs decimal prefixes (MiB vs MB), process RSS vs heap.
pitfall: Numbers that look comparable but are not

text: When distributions are skewed, multi-modal or have outliers, show them (box, violin or cumulative distribution plots) rather than only a mean with error bars.
pitfall: Averages hiding the real behaviour

text: Show reference points that make scores readable where they exist: floor and ceiling, random or trivial baseline, human level, theoretical upper bound.
pitfall: Scores with no sense of what is good or bad

text: Never headline a best case alone ("up to 10× faster"): state the aggregate together with the best and worst results.
pitfall: A single favourable sub-result sold as the conclusion

text: Ask the user which decision the benchmark must inform before designing anything.
pitfall: Measuring first and choosing the conclusion after

text: Phrase the goal neutrally ("which option fits this case"), never "show that X wins", as one short question of 80 characters at most: the page and the README card show it as their title.
pitfall: Biased goals steer workload and metric choices

text: Derive candidate metrics from what the system delivers; the user picks and weights them, the agent proposes and challenges.
pitfall: Irrelevant or convenient metrics
proved_by: metrics[] (label, kind, unit, direction, statistic, weight)

text: Before designing, research the domain: existing reference benchmarks or suites, standard metrics and units, and known pitfalls, from your own knowledge first, then a web search when available. Prefer reusing a reference suite; if it is subset, justify each omission and never report an overall score for the subset. Record what was found, or that nothing was found.
pitfall: Ignoring what the domain already knows; cherry-picked subsets
proved_by: domain_research (reference suites, metrics, pitfalls, sources; may be empty)

text: Use a workload representative of the user's real use: the input ranges that matter and the way the system is actually called (one request or many, batch or sequential), since the usage pattern can change cost and speed by an order of magnitude (Kapoor et al.).
pitfall: Input ranges chosen to make one option look good

text: Show where each option improves and where it degrades (progressive and conservative criteria).
pitfall: Hiding the trade-off

text: Compare against the right baseline: the current state of the art or an unperturbed system, not an old version or yourself.
pitfall: Inflated gains from outdated baselines

text: Give every competitor the same tuning effort, document every configuration, disable debug defaults, and enable the features a production user would turn on.
pitfall: Unfairly configured competitors

text: Keep tuning or calibration data disjoint from evaluation data, and hold out items at the level of generality you claim: new tasks for a general claim, not just new examples (Kapoor et al.).
pitfall: Results that only show fit to known data

text: Benchmark actively: observe the system during runs and answer the sanity checklist (why not double, was it tuned, did it break limits, did it error, does it reproduce, does it matter, did it even happen).
pitfall: Measuring the wrong bottleneck or a run that never happened

text: Record hardware, software versions, configuration and where the measurements ran (bare metal, a virtual machine, a container, a CI runner), and write down assumptions and limitations.
pitfall: Results nobody can interpret or reproduce

text: State what the benchmark tests and how its scores should be interpreted.
pitfall: Scores read as broader claims than they support

text: Run a sensitivity check: vary the parameters most likely to matter (input size, concurrency, settings) and say whether the conclusion holds.
pitfall: Conclusions that only hold at one setting

text: Before publishing, look for clauses restricting benchmark publication ("DeWitt clauses") in each candidate's licence or terms of service, quote and link any clause found, and tell the user before anything is published. Offer the options (ask the vendor for permission, keep that candidate private, or decide knowingly), say that enforceability varies by jurisdiction (a New York court struck down one such clause), and state plainly that this is not legal advice. Record the address of the terms read and the date, also when nothing was found.
pitfall: Publishing results a licence forbids, or silently dropping inconvenient candidates

text: For services you do not control (SaaS, APIs, cloud), timestamp every measurement, record region, plan and version, spread runs across times of day and days, and aim for claims that would hold on a rerun rather than identical numbers.
pitfall: Results tied to one moment, one region or one silent update

text: Publish the scripts, configuration and raw data needed to rerun the benchmark, with the exact commands, and link them from every output.
pitfall: Results nobody can check or rerun

text: Version the benchmark itself: any change to workload, metrics or scoring creates a new version, and results from different versions are never compared directly.
pitfall: Numbers from different benchmarks compared under one name

text: Have the program that measures write the raw data, one line per observation, failures included: your own script, or a tool's export converted by astrolabe import. Never type or copy a measured number yourself, and never compute a statistic: run astrolabe compute.
pitfall: Numbers miscopied, rounded or invented by the agent; intervals computed wrongly by hand

text: Publish only when the user asks. Never push, change repository settings or create an account on your own initiative
Look before asking: an existing workflow, host config file, custom-domain file or documentation site tells which case applies. Propose that host; ask only when nothing is found
Never replace a site that already exists. Publish in a sub-folder of it

Before the first publication, tell the user what becomes public: the page, `benchmark.json` and the raw data files. Check the raw data for secrets and personal data, and say so when the repository is private
Nothing is published from a file that fails `validate`
In CI, run the version the project pins: install the project's dependencies (`npm ci`, or the install step its other workflows use), then `npx --no-install astrolabe`

After publication, open the address and check four things: the page loads with its styles, a filter changes the chart, an evidence link opens, and the hash shown on the page is the one `validate` prints
Once the address is known, set `--url` in the build command and add the link to the README
Give the user the steps only they can do as a short numbered list, with the exact names of the settings
Prefer blind pairwise comparisons (which of A and B is better, tie allowed) for subtle differences; absolute ratings scale better but drift more when the judge changes.
pitfall: Drifting, poorly calibrated scales

text: Hide candidate identities and randomize presentation order. For scores gathered before the plan without either, declare what was done (`blinded: false`, the order used): every verdict that rests on them then says the judges knew.
pitfall: Brand and position bias

text: Sample all candidates evenly and keep the comparison graph connected.
pitfall: Unequal exposure distorting rankings

text: Publish every variant tested, not only the best one, with the total number tried; no retracting scores (see S9).
pitfall: Selection bias from best-of-many testing

text: When judges are models, apply the quality.md judge rules (Q6–Q8, Q11).
pitfall: Judge biases

text: With several raters judging the same items, have a subset rated twice and report Krippendorff's alpha: at or above 0.8 is reliable, 0.667–0.8 supports only tentative conclusions, below 0.667 the ratings should not be used. These cut-offs are conventions, not laws. People scoring the candidates for their own taste are participants, not raters, and need no agreement figure; ratings gathered before the plan without a double-rated subset are of unknown reliability, and validate warns.
pitfall: Conclusions drawn from inconsistent ratings

text: Accept an automated judge only if it agrees with humans about as well as humans agree with each other on the same items.
pitfall: A proxy that is worse than the people it replaces

text: When items come in related groups, use clustered standard errors and report the number of clusters (naive errors can be several times too small).
pitfall: Error bars that are too narrow

text: For non-deterministic candidates, run each item several times, average per item, and compute the error from per-item means (never pool all answers as independent).
pitfall: One lucky or unlucky run decides the ranking

text: Verify outputs are actually correct (read back what was written, check each answer), not just that the run completed.
pitfall: Counting wrong or empty outputs as successes

text: When a model judges two outputs, judge both orders and count a win only when both agree (otherwise a tie); random order assignment is an alternative at large scale.
pitfall: Position bias

text: Never let a candidate, or a model from the same family, judge its own outputs; test the judge for verbosity bias (a padded copy of an answer must not win).
pitfall: Self-preference and verbosity bias

text: Validate an automated judge against a sample of human ratings before trusting it.
pitfall: An unvalidated proxy treated as ground truth

text: Never report one aggregate alone: show sub-scores per task family.
pitfall: Averages hiding regressions

text: Check whether candidates may already have seen the test items (public test sets in training data, or tuning on the same public set); prefer fresh, private or regenerated items and state which were used.
pitfall: Memorization scored as capability

text: For items with a verifiable answer, check automatically or give the judge a reference answer instead of letting it grade freely.
pitfall: Judges misled by wrong candidate answers

text: Do not change a candidate's sampling settings (e.g. temperature) just to reduce variance; repeat items instead, unless the user's real use runs with those settings.
pitfall: Measuring a different system, or adding bias

text: Measure total resource use, including work offloaded to other cores, processes or services.
pitfall: Hiding cost on a "free" core

text: Express changes in usage as relative increases, not percentage-point differences (6% to 13% is more than double, not +7%).
pitfall: Downplayed overhead

text: Start from a quiescent system and verify it stays quiet; record background load.
pitfall: Noise from other activity

text: For energy, state which domain the counter covers (e.g. RAPL package, cores or DRAM) and that it is not whole-machine power.
pitfall: Partial energy reported as total

text: For energy, control and report frequency scaling and thread affinity, and report the average frequency actually reached.
pitfall: Results driven by clock behaviour rather than the code

text: Do not rely only on an automated script for energy: form an expected result first and check the measurements against it.
pitfall: Undetected counter or tooling errors

text: Check results against theoretical limits (hardware maximums); a result beyond them is an error.
pitfall: Impossible numbers published
proved_by: enforced by the generator against a ceiling declared in metrics[].reference_points

text: Name the memory metric exactly: peak, steady state or residual after the operation; process RSS (includes runtime overhead and memory not returned to the OS) or language heap. Never compare different definitions.
pitfall: Comparing numbers that measure different things

text: Sample memory repeatedly during the run instead of taking one snapshot; report peak, steady state and growth.
pitfall: Missing transient peaks or slow leaks

text: For garbage-collected runtimes, treat heap size and GC settings as a factor: record them, and compare at several heap sizes when memory matters.
pitfall: Rankings that flip with heap size

text: For managed runtimes, account for JIT warm-up and adaptive-optimization nondeterminism (see T1 and S4).
pitfall: Measuring the warm-up instead of the steady state

text: Report variability (SD or CI) and sample size next to every compared value, in text and charts.
pitfall: Noise presented as signal
proved_by: values[] (n, value, sd, ci, ci_level), metrics[].statistic

text: Compare on paired data where possible (same items, same inputs) and report the difference, its standard error, its CI and the correlation between candidates.
pitfall: Overstated or missed differences

text: Compute ratios and speedups with the baseline in the denominator, with their own CI (e.g. Fieller's interval).
pitfall: Gains inflated by the reference point

text: Repeat at every level where variance appears (build, process, iteration), most where most variance occurs; repetition at the highest variable level is mandatory.
pitfall: False precision

text: Round values to what their variability supports.
pitfall: Pseudo-accuracy

text: Prefer robust statistics (median, percentiles) to removing outliers. If removal is unavoidable, declare the rule in the plan before measuring (`analysis.outliers`, e.g. Tukey's 1.5 × IQR): compute applies it and reports how many values were removed. Never delete rows from a raw file.
pitfall: Inconvenient results quietly removed

text: State conclusions as effect sizes with confidence intervals ("A is faster than B by 5.5% ± 2.5%"), compared with the user's minimum meaningful difference. Non-overlapping CIs do indicate a difference, but overlapping CIs prove nothing; prefer the CI of the difference over p-values or visual overlap. The effect, its interval and the verdict, with the qualifier "likely" when part of the interval falls short of the minimum, are computed by astrolabe compute.
pitfall: "Statistically significant" but irrelevant, or misread tests

text: Before the full run, estimate the minimum detectable effect from a pilot; if the benchmark cannot detect the difference the user cares about, enlarge it or say so.
pitfall: Running a benchmark that cannot answer the question

text: When several variants or configurations were tried, report how many, and re-measure the selected one on fresh runs or data before presenting it.
pitfall: Best-of-N selection inflating the result

text: Do not assume normal distributions because the sample is large: performance data is usually skewed and multi-modal. Check (Q-Q plot, Shapiro-Wilk) before using mean-based CIs, or use the median with a nonparametric CI (needs more than 5 samples).
pitfall: Tight-looking CIs around a mean that represents nothing

text: Declare the primary comparisons in the plan, before measuring, and keep them few. Their intervals are widened together (Bonferroni) and only they may carry a headline; every other comparison is labelled exploratory. State how many comparisons of each kind were made.
pitfall: "Better" verdicts that appear by chance among many candidates, metrics and nodes

text: Run untimed warm-up iterations, and decide explicitly whether the user cares about cold or warm performance (use a prepare step to reset caches for cold runs).
pitfall: Mixing cold and warm states

text: Randomize or vary incidental setup (run order, environment, layout) and interleave configurations rather than running them in blocks.
pitfall: Measurement bias from "innocuous" setup choices

text: For latency, report percentiles or the full distribution, not only the mean; never average percentiles across workers or windows, merge histograms instead (histograms add up, percentiles do not). Compare at the percentiles that matter: one system can win at the median and lose at p99 (Hoefler & Belli, rule 8).
pitfall: Hidden tail latency, mathematically wrong aggregates

text: For load tests, use an open model (fixed arrival rate) and measure each request from the time it was scheduled to be sent, so slow responses do not reduce the load or hide the wait.
pitfall: Coordinated omission hiding the worst latencies

text: Separate successful and failed requests before reading latency; check that runs did not error out.
pitfall: Fast failures counted as fast results

text: Pair throughput with resource usage (CPU per request or per byte); a throughput drop of x% is not an overhead of x%.
pitfall: Understated overhead

text: Do not present micro-benchmarks as overall performance; add a realistic end-to-end workload.
pitfall: Kernel results sold as application results

text: Keep timer overhead under 5% of the measured interval and timer resolution at least 10 times finer (Hoefler & Belli); time single events when the timer allows, since batching loses percentiles and per-event CIs, and remove harness overhead.
pitfall: Timer and harness noise in the result

text: Prefer established tools that handle warm-up, repetition and outlier detection (e.g. hyperfine for commands, wrk2 for HTTP load).
pitfall: Hand-rolled timing mistakes

text: Compare the run time, memory, CPU or energy of a suite script by script. One figure for scripts of different sizes either pools their runs, so its median belongs to none of them, or averages them, so the longest decide the change: either way a slower script can hide behind faster ones.
pitfall: A suite figure that hides one script getting slower behind others getting faster

text: Define representative tasks with explicit success criteria before testing, and state who the users are (novice or expert) and the context.
pitfall: Tasks chosen to flatter one tool

text: Measure effectiveness (task success, errors), efficiency (time on task) and satisfaction (e.g. SUS) separately, and report all three.
pitfall: Collapsing weakly related measures into one score

text: Count time on failed tasks separately from successful ones. A time measured on successful attempts only is labelled so, and compared next to the failure rate: a candidate that gives up on hard tasks looks faster (compute warns when the failure shares differ).
pitfall: Fast abandonment counted as efficiency

text: Verify each claimed feature by actually using it; record present, partial or absent with evidence and the product version and date.
pitfall: Marketing pages taken as facts

text: In weighted feature matrices, let the user set the weights (F3), define each scoring scale, always show the per-criterion scores beside the total, and run a weight sensitivity check; note that adding or removing an option can reverse the ranking.
pitfall: Totals driven by arbitrary weights or scales

text: To compare usability numbers, test at least 20 participants per condition (around 40 for tight intervals). Five users find problems; they cannot rank products. With fewer participants, label results as indicative and declare no winner.
pitfall: Rankings built on qualitative-size samples

text: Choose the chart from the data shape in the table above, and encode the compared quantity as a position on a common scale before any other encoding.
pitfall: A chart picked for looks that readers judge less accurately

text: Do not use angle or area (pie, donut, bubble size) to compare candidates.
pitfall: Judgments by angle and circular area are less accurate than by position

text: Do not chart one, two or three numbers: use a headline block or a sentence.
pitfall: A chart that adds ink but no information

text: Beyond 8 candidates in one chart, highlight the subject and grey the rest, or split into small multiples; never add colours.
pitfall: Colours that can no longer be told apart

text: Never put two metrics on two y-axes of one chart; use two charts side by side, an indexed chart or a scatter.
pitfall: An apparent relation that only comes from the choice of scales

text: Panels meant to be compared share the same scale; when they cannot, say so in each panel.
pitfall: Small panels that look alike but differ by an order of magnitude

text: Mark the direction on every chart ("lower is better"), taken from the metric, never typed by hand. Never invert an axis so that lower values look bigger; state the direction and sort best-first instead.
pitfall: A reader who takes the longest bar for the winner

text: When an axis does not start at zero, set its range from the minimum meaningful difference, so that a difference of that size is visible but a smaller one does not look large.
pitfall: The designer choosing, without saying so, how important a difference looks

text: Use a linear scale by default. A log scale needs a reason written in `scale.reason` (values spanning orders of magnitude, a long-tailed distribution such as latencies, a question about ratios). The generator then writes "log scale" in the axis title, labels ticks with real values (1, 10, 100) and refuses bars.
pitfall: A scale most readers misread, chosen without saying why; bar lengths that mean nothing without a zero

text: Sort candidates best-first according to the metric's direction, or keep one declared order on every chart of the page; never choose the order chart by chart to favour one candidate.
pitfall: The subject always shown first or last by construction

text: Draw the interval on every charted value that has one, and name it in the chart with its real level, read from `ci_level` ("95% confidence interval, 10 runs"; "98.75% interval, adjusted for 4 primary comparisons").
pitfall: Error bars read as something else: standard error, standard deviation and confidence interval look the same

text: When the point of the chart is a comparison, prefer a dot with its interval to a bar with an error bar.
pitfall: Values inside the bar are judged likelier than values above it, and the interval is read as all-or-nothing

text: To show who wins, chart the difference itself with its interval and the minimum meaningful difference as a band, rather than leaving the reader to compare two overlapping intervals. When the comparison is paired, two separate intervals cannot show the result at all: the page must then show it as an effect chart, a comparison-rows chart or a headline.
pitfall: Winners read from overlapping or non-overlapping error bars

text: When the reader's question is what one run or one request will look like (latency, flaky tasks), show the spread of outcomes (distribution, percentiles), not only the interval of the mean.
pitfall: A narrow confidence interval read as "every run is better": readers overestimate the effect and underestimate variability

text: With few measurements per candidate (about 10 or fewer), plot every point next to the summary.
pitfall: The same mean and error bar produced by very different data (an outlier, two clusters, three points)

text: Write colours only in `style`, never in a block: a theme, an accent, optional colours per candidate. Leave every derived colour to the generator.
pitfall: Hand-picked colours that break in dark mode, in an export or after a theme change

text: Give each candidate one colour and keep it on every chart, table marker and export of the page; unlisted candidates take the theme's colours in the order of `candidates[]`.
pitfall: A reader relearning the legend on each chart, or the same colour meaning two things

text: Never let colour be the only way to tell candidates apart: label them directly on the chart, and vary line style or marker shape.
pitfall: Charts unreadable for the roughly 8% of men with a colour-vision deficiency, or in greyscale

text: Marks needed to read the chart have a contrast of at least 3:1 against what is next to them, text at least 4.5:1. The generator checks the user's colours in both modes and adjusts their lightness, or refuses.
pitfall: Brand colours that vanish on the background

text: Use at most 8 distinct colours in one chart.
pitfall: Colours too close to be matched to their label

text: When the page is about one candidate (the user's own project), name it in `highlight`: it takes the accent and the others take greys. Its rank, value and interval are drawn exactly like the others.
pitfall: Every candidate shouting equally, or emphasis obtained by distorting the data

text: Keep one reserved pair of colours for better and worse, always with a sign or a word, and never give those colours to a candidate. Do not use red against green.
pitfall: A candidate that looks "bad" because of its colour; a verdict invisible to colour-blind readers

text: For ordered values (shaded tables, heat maps) use one hue going from light to dark; use two hues only around a meaningful midpoint such as zero difference; never a rainbow scale.
pitfall: Equal steps that look unequal, and a bright band that draws the eye to arbitrary values

text: Let the generator produce the light and dark variants from the same `style`; `mode` is `auto`, `light` or `dark`.
pitfall: A page that is only legible in the mode its author used

text: Write titles that state the finding in 60 characters at most as the reader sees them, and list in `asserts` the verdicts the title relies on. Use "better" words only for a better verdict, "same" only for equivalent, and say inconclusive when it is. Rely only on primary comparisons (S11); an exploratory one never makes a headline or a claim in a title.
pitfall: A slanted title that readers remember instead of the data, and that survives a rerun that no longer supports it

text: Never type a result into a title or description: insert it with a template (`{effect:id}`, `{verdict:id}`, `{candidate:id}`).
pitfall: Figures left over from a previous run

text: Under every chart, say how to read it: what is measured, the unit, the direction, the number of items and runs, and what the interval is. The generator writes this line from `results`.
pitfall: A chart that cannot be read without the page around it

text: Label candidates on the chart itself instead of a separate legend. Put the overall message in the title, and statistics or context next to the data point they describe.
pitfall: Eyes going back and forth to a legend; a message stated far from its evidence

text: Lay tables out for comparison: numbers right-aligned with the same number of decimals down a column, text left-aligned, the unit once in the header, headers set apart, light dividers, the row or cell that matters highlighted.
pitfall: Numbers that cannot be compared by eye down a column

text: Show no more digits than the uncertainty supports: round a value to the decimal of the first significant digit of its standard error, and show the interval with the same decimals. Percentages: whole numbers, one decimal below 10%.
pitfall: 82.4137% displayed for a result known to within 5 points

text: In any table of results, keep the columns that let the reader judge the number: items, runs, interval, failures.
pitfall: A bare score with nothing to weigh it by

text: When a table grows past about 20 rows or 8 columns, shade the cells (V23), sort it, or replace it with a chart; keep the full table one click away.
pitfall: A wall of numbers nobody reads

text: Make the default state of every filter the one that carries the message, and never put a result that matters behind a click or a hover. Every `asserts` must hold in the default state.
pitfall: The main finding seen by a small minority of readers

text: Use tooltips only to repeat or detail values that are also in the chart labels or in the data table.
pitfall: Values out of reach on touch screens, by keyboard or in an image

text: When a filter changes the data shown, keep the axis fixed across its options; if the range must change, show that it did.
pitfall: Two filter states compared by eye on two different scales

text: Keep the filter state in the page address, so a link reproduces exactly what its sender saw.
pitfall: A shared link showing something else than what was discussed

text: Use a filter only when one view cannot hold the content; a breakdown that fits on the page is shown, not filtered.
pitfall: Controls added for their own sake

text: Order the page from the answer to the evidence: headline or summary blocks, the chart that backs them, the breakdowns, the full table, then the trust blocks.
pitfall: A reader who has to scroll past method to find the result, or who never reaches the evidence

text: Put at most two blocks in a row, three when they are all headline or summary blocks, and at most three headline and summary blocks on a page; rows stack into one column on narrow screens.
pitfall: Charts too small to read; a headline row where nothing stands out

text: Give each chart one message. When too many elements compete in one chart, split it, aggregate, or filter.
pitfall: A chart that shows everything and says nothing

text: Make every export readable alone: title, candidate names, unit, direction, and the interval note are inside the image.
pitfall: A chart shared on a social site with no way to know what it measures

text: Print a provenance line in every export: where the full page is, the short hash of `results`, the date.
pitfall: A number that cannot be traced back to its data

text: An export shows the default state of the filters, or a state named in its preset; never a state picked by hand at export time.
pitfall: The most flattering slice exported without saying it is a slice

text: In the Markdown report, give every value its interval, its number of runs and its failures in the table: the report draws no chart, so its tables carry the uncertainty.
pitfall: A Markdown export that silently drops the uncertainty

text: Ask for both modes of a README card unless the user wants one; give every exported image a generated alt text (V46).
pitfall: A dark card on a light page; an image with no description

text: Every chart has a text alternative in two parts: a short one naming the chart, and a longer one, visible to everyone, giving scales, values and the trend. The generator writes the factual part from `results` (what is plotted, extremes, comparisons); the agent's `description` adds the reading.
pitfall: A chart that says nothing to a screen reader, or an alt text that only says "bar chart"

text: Every chart can show its data as a table.
pitfall: Values that exist only as shapes

text: Filters and any other control work with the keyboard and show focus; nothing needs a mouse.
pitfall: Controls out of reach without a pointer

text: No text below 12 px at the size the chart is shown, exports included.
pitfall: Axis labels unreadable once a chart is shrunk into a card

text: Animation is optional decoration: it is switched off when the reader asks for reduced motion, and nothing flashes.
pitfall: Motion that harms or distracts, and content that only appears after an animation

text: Leave the "Built with" mention on by default, inside the provenance line: small muted text, no logo, never over the data. Remove it only when the user asks, by setting `style.attribution` to false; the hash, date and source link stay. Never word it as a verification.
pitfall: A mention that reads as an advert or a certification, or that comes back on the next build because it was removed by a command-line flag

text: Use stacked bars only to show the parts of one total. To compare one part across candidates, use grouped bars or one chart per part. Radar and 3D charts are not in the chart set.
pitfall: A part compared across floating segments, which readers judge far less accurately than aligned bars

text: On narrow screens, redraw each chart rather than shrink it: horizontal bars, fewer ticks, shorter labels, annotations shortened or moved below. Never drop the interval, the direction or a candidate.
pitfall: Text too small to read on a phone, or a phone version that silently loses the uncertainty
proved_by: the generator renders a narrow version of every chart

text: Use comparison-rows when several metrics are each compared once with the baseline. Each row is one comparison: the baseline as a grey track and the candidate as a bar, both from zero on the row's own scale; the two values with their intervals; the effect with its interval. A row whose verdict is equivalent or inconclusive shows that word instead of an effect figure. The chart says that each row has its own scale. Beyond about 10 rows, use a table.
pitfall: A stack of impressive figures with no uncertainty, a row that did not improve hidden among wins, or rows of different units read as one scale

text: Show a relative effect as a factor (effect_format: times) only when the effects are large, about 2× or more; below that, a percentage reads better (+20% rather than 1.2×). The generator computes the factor and its interval from the comparison, larger value over smaller, and writes what it is a factor of: faster or slower for time, less or more for resources, cheaper or more expensive for cost, higher or lower otherwise. Never a bare × on a worse result.
pitfall: 1.2× read as a large change; 0.35× read as a gain; a factor that disagrees with the values printed next to it
proved_by: blocks[].effect_format (times only on relative comparisons, checked)

text: Never present a declared figure like a computed one. The generator marks every declared value "declared" wherever it appears (label, table cell, headline, export), writes "likely" and "exploratory" with the verdicts they qualify, writes "successful attempts only" next to every result that leaves failures out and a visible warning when the candidates' failure shares differ, and lists in the methodology block what was computed from raw data and what was only declared, with the number of comparisons of each kind.
pitfall: A typed-in figure or an unchecked declaration read with the same trust as a computed result
